body.heading: A material born in furnaces
paragraphs: Glass begins as sand — mostly silica — heated with soda ash and lime until, at around 1,300 to 1,600 degrees Celsius, it melts into a glowing liquid that cools into a hard, transparent solid. Nature makes it too, where lightning strikes sand or volcanoes erupt, but deliberate glassmaking began about 3,600 years ago in Mesopotamia and Egypt.
The earliest glass was a luxury, coloured like gemstones and shaped by wrapping molten strands around a core of clay. A single small bottle could be a treasure, traded across the ancient world.

body.heading: The blowpipe changes everything
paragraphs: Around the 1st century BC, craftspeople on the Syro-Palestinian coast discovered glassblowing: gather a blob of molten glass on a hollow pipe, blow, and a vessel inflates like a bubble. Glass became fast and cheap to shape, and for the first time ordinary Roman households could own glass cups and bottles.

Glassmakers guarded their recipes fiercely. Venice moved its furnaces to the island of Murano in 1291 — officially against fire risk, and conveniently keeping its masters of crystal-clear glass where rivals could not easily hire them away.

body.heading: The material science looks through
paragraphs: Clear, flat glass remade daily life: windows that admit light but not weather, mirrors, spectacles that gave ageing scholars back their reading, and lenses that opened two new worlds — the telescope's planets and the microscope's microbes.
Today glass carries our messages as optical fibres and faces us in every screen. Sand, soda, lime and fire: still the recipe, still astonishing.

takeaway: Glassblowing turned a luxury of kings into an everyday material, and its clarity went on to power telescopes, microscopes and modern screens.
